# Full-Response handoff byte vectors

`vectors.json` compares complete domain-framed handoff bytes across TypeScript `canonicalResponseHandoffBytes` and Rust `canonical_response_handoff_bytes`. The fixture contains raw JSON inputs, canonical JSON, hexadecimal framed bytes and SHA-256. Positive cases cover equivalent key order, Unicode/UTF-16 property order, number formatting (including literal -0), exact 19-significant-digit decimals and an integer above 2^53 written several ways, and preservation of full signature/receipt/metadata/locale values. Negative wire cases reject non-object roots, malformed JSON, lone surrogate values/keys and numbers outside the binary64 range.

Signature evidence in these synthetic byte inputs is not cryptographically valid; these tests establish preservation, not signing-method validity or schema conformance. Constructed JS non-JSON values (undefined, BigInt, cycles, etc.) live in the TS tests because they cannot be represented by wire JSON fixtures.

Numbers follow `integrity-canonical-json-v1`: the exact decimal value in ECMAScript `Number::toString` layout. That equals RFC 8785 whenever the text is the shortest decimal that round-trips to its double, so `333333333.33333329` keeps all its digits where RFC 8785 writes `333333333.3333333`. Regenerate independently with Python `rfc8785` 0.1.4, `../exact_jcs.py` (its own number reader and layout; it asserts agreement with `rfc8785` wherever the text is its double's shortest form) and standard-library `hashlib`:

```sh
python3 tests/fixtures/response-handoff/generate.py
```

The generator imports no Rust/TypeScript code and does not read expected vector output. It must run in an environment with the documented reference installed; it installs nothing. Compare committed output after reproduction.

Primary sources: [RFC 8785](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc8785), [Trail of Bits Python reference](https://github.com/trailofbits/rfc8785.py), [canonicalize JavaScript implementation](https://github.com/erdtman/canonicalize). Neither runtime uses a third-party canonicalizer: RFC 8785 rounds numbers, so both carry the exact-number writer. No generated bytes authorize any cryptographic signing or public release.
